chunks: ʿAbd al-Wāḥid ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAbdūs al-Naysābūrī, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated from ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad ibn Qutaybah, from Ḥamdān ibn Sulaymān, from ʿAbd al-Salām ibn Ṣāliḥ al-Harawī, who said:

I said to al-Riḍā عليه السلام: O son of the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم, it has been narrated to us from your forefathers عليهم السلام that concerning one who has intercourse in the month of Ramaḍān or breaks the fast in it, there are three expiations. And it has also been narrated from them عليهم السلام: one expiation. So which of the two reports should we follow?

He said: Both of them. Whenever a man has unlawful intercourse or breaks his fast with something unlawful in the month of Ramaḍān, then three expiations are due from him: freeing a slave, fasting two consecutive months, and feeding sixty needy persons, along with making up that day. And if he had lawful intercourse or broke his fast with something lawful, then one expiation is due from him along with making up that day. And if he was forgetful, then nothing is due from him.

key_terms.إِطْعَامُ سِتِّينَ مِسْكِيناً: feeding sixty needy persons as expiation
key_terms.حَرَاماً: that which is religiously forbidden, making the violation more severe
key_terms.صِيَامُ شَهْرَيْنِ مُتَتَابِعَيْنِ: fasting two consecutive months as expiation
key_terms.عِتْقُ رَقَبَةٍ: freeing a slave as one form of expiation
key_terms.قَضَاءُ ذَلِكَ الْيَوْمِ: making up the invalidated fast of that day
key_terms.كَفَّارَاتٍ: expiations required as compensation for violating the fast
key_terms.نَاسِياً: acting out of forgetfulness, which removes liability here

ai.seo_question: When does breaking a fast in Ramaḍān require one kaffarah versus three kaffarahs?
ai.summary: This hadith explains how two outwardly different reports about kaffarah for violating the fast of Ramaḍān are reconciled. The ruling is that three expiations apply when the violation involves something haram, while one expiation applies when the act itself was halal in origin, and in both cases the fast of that day must be made up; no liability applies in forgetfulness.
